Lateral Collateral Ligament and Posterolateral Corner Injuries
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Injuries to the lateral collateral ligament (LCL) and posterolateral corner (PLC) are less common
than injuries to the medial side of the knee, partly because of lack of recognition.
Associated with injuries to the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) and posterior cruciate ligament
(PCL)
Epidemiology
Lateral-sided ligament injuries are observed in 16% of all knee ligament injuries.
Only 28% of PLC injuries occur in isolation.
2.1% of ligament injuries are isolated LCL/PLC injuries.
9.1% of all patients with acute hemarthrosis have a PLC injury.

Epidemiology
Isolated PLC injuries are rare and often occur in the setting of concomitant pathology.
LaPrade et al1 published a prospective MRI study on patients with an acute knee injury
and hemarthrosis. Overall, 9.1% of all MRIs of patients with an acute hemarthrosis
revealed a PLC injury. Of the MRIs on which a ligament injury was observed, 67% of the
injuries were isolated, whereas one-third of the injuries involved multiple ligaments.
Only 2.1% of patients with a ligament injury had an isolated PLC injury. Disruption of the
PLC was observed on 16% of the MRIs of patients with a ligament injury, indicating that
the PLC is most often torn in combination with other ligaments.1 To further assess
concomitant injury, Geeslin and LaPrade2 performed a retrospective study evaluating at
the characteristics of a series of managed PLC injuries. The authors found that isolated

Anatomy
Primary Static Stabilizers
LCL: originates proximal and posterior to the lateral femoral condyle and inserts most
anteriorly on the fibular head at approximately the middle (Figure 1)
Popliteofibular ligament: originates at the myotendinous junction of the popliteus and inserts
on the posteromedial aspect of the fibular styloid anterior to the biceps femoris and posterior
to the LCL
Popliteal tendon: deep, anterior, and distal to the LCL origin in the popliteal sulcus of the distal
femur and inserts on the posterior tibia
Dynamic Stabilizers and Secondary Static Stabilizers
Iliotibial band: inserts on the Gerdy tubercle; superficial structure.
Lateral gastrocnemius tendon
Biceps femoris
Mid-third lateral capsular ligament: similar to the deep medial collateral ligament (MCL) of the
medial knee
Coronary ligament
Fabellofibular ligament

Dynamic Stabilizers and Secondary Static Stabilizers
Seebacher et al3 proposed a three-layer description of the soft-tissue structures of the
lateral knee. More recent anatomic descriptions have made important refinements that
provide the basis for reconstruction of the posterolateral structures. The term arcuate
ligament has been supplanted by a more nuanced description of the popliteofibular and
fabellofibular ligaments; the term has been used to describe several structures about
the lateral knee, including the popliteofibular ligament and the fabellofibular ligament.4
Terry and LaPrade5 and LaPrade et al6 published a comprehensive anatomic study
assessing the femoral, tibial, and fibular attachments for the lateral structures of the
knee. The lateral (or fibular) collateral ligament is 4 to 5 mm in width and originates on
the lateral femur 1.4 mm proximal and 3.1 mm posterior to the lateral femoral
epicondyle.4 The length of the LCL is 62.6 to 73.5 mm.6 The popliteal muscle inserts on

structure as it travels proximally and laterally about the lateral third of the tibia. The
popliteal tendon courses intra-articularly through the popliteal hiatus of the coronary
ligament before inserting on the lateral distal femur.7 The popliteal insertion on the
femur is distal, anterior, and deep to the LCL, with the mean distance between them
being 18.5 mm.6 The popliteofibular ligament forms from the myotendinous junction of
the popliteus and takes off at a mean angle of 83° to attach within close proximity to the
fibular styloid.6 The tendon has two divisions: posterior and anterior6 (Resource 1; Video

The primary attachment of the iliotibial band is the Gerdy tubercle on the tibia; however,
it has other attachments to the distal femur and patella. An important concept of the
iliotibial band is that, in extension, it has an extension moment about the knee because
it is anterior to the hinge point of the knee; in flexion, its moment is posterior to the
hinge point, making it a flexor. This phenomenon explains the pivot-shift test in patients
with an ACL rupture, in which the tibia is being reduced by the flexion moment of the
iliotibial band.

The lateral head of the gastrocnemius courses proximally and encases the fabella or a
cartilaginous analog before adhering to the posterior meniscofemoral capsule and
attaching on or near the supracondylar process of the distal femur.6 The distance from
the lateral gastrocnemius attachment to the LCL origin and the lateral epicondyle is 13.8
and 17.2 mm, respectively.6
The biceps femoris has a long head and a short head. The long head of the biceps
femoris has two attachment arms that include the direct arm and the anterior arm. The
direct arm attaches to the posterior aspect of the fibular head, whereas the anterior arm
crosses over the LCL to attach to the fibula anterior to the LCL. A biceps bursa lies
between the anterior arm and the LCL.8 The short head of the biceps has multiple
attachments, most notably to the long head of the biceps and the capsular arm, which is
known as the fabellofibular ligament. The fabellofibular ligament is inconsistently
reported in cadaver model studies; however, it is the distal extent of the capsular arm of
the short head of the biceps and inserts near the lateral aspect of the fibular styloid.4
This ligament is tight in extension and thought to provide some lateral knee stability in
extension.9
The mid-third lateral capsular ligament has been described as the deep MCL (dMCL) of
the lateral knee. This area of thickened capsule spans from the supracondylar process to
just anterior to the lateral epicondyle on the femur and distally inserts, spanning from
the anterior portion of the popliteal hiatus to the posterior aspect of the Gerdy
tubercle.4 The meniscofemoral and meniscotibial ligaments are portions of this ligament
that are responsible for securing the lateral meniscus to the capsule. Segond fractures
are thought to be avulsions of the mid-third lateral capsule. The coronary ligament is
located in the posterior aspect of the capsule and is a meniscotibial ligament responsible
for securing the posterior root of the lateral meniscus to the tibial plateau.4

Neurovascular Structures
The common peroneal nerve is located posterior to the biceps femoris and often is
released during PLC reconstruction (Figure 2). It is commonly injured in patients with a
PLC injury; therefore, a neurovascular examination must be thoroughly documented.
Lastly, the inferior lateral geniculate artery is the major blood supply in the lateral part of
the knee. Clinically, inferior lateral geniculate artery may aid in identifying injured
structures on MRI because it reliably passes from medial to lateral between the
popliteofibular ligament and the fabellofibular ligament.4

Biomechanics
LCL: primarily resists varus
Popliteofibular ligament: resists external tibial rotation
Popliteal tendon: technically a dynamic/static stabilizer; primarily resists external rotation;
secondary restraint to varus.
Concave-on-concave osseous surfaces

Biomechanics
The osseous morphology of the lateral side of the knee consists of two concave-shaped
surfaces; this makes the lateral knee inherently dependent on soft-tissue support for
stability.10 This principle allows most MCL injuries to be successfully managed
nonsurgically, whereas unaddressed PLC injuries often result in persistent pain and
instability.
The primary role of the LCL is to resist varus.7,11,12 Sectioning of the popliteus also has a
secondary role in varus stabilization.13 The popliteofibular ligament and the lateral
capsule are secondary contributors in resisting varus.4 The ACL and PCL are recruited to
resist varus if the PLC is incompetent.4 This explains the reason unrecognized PLC
injuries are associated with higher failure rates in patients who undergo ACL
reconstruction.
The popliteus plays an important role in external rotation because it is one of the
primary restraints to external rotation and a checkrein against anterior translation of the
tibia.13 The popliteofibular ligament is a primary restraint to external rotation.11
Between 0° and 30° of knee flexion, the LCL is the primary restraint to external rotation;

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Sporting activities and motorcycle and motor vehicle collisions are the most common causes.
The main mechanisms of injury include a varus blow to a flexed knee, isolated hyperextension,
hyperextension in combination with external rotation, and frank knee dislocation.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Multiple studies have identified sporting activities as the most common circumstance in
which PLC injury occurs (40% to 65% of cases), followed by motor vehicle collisions.16,18
A commonly described mechanism of injury usually involves a posterolaterally directed
force on the anteromedial tibia.16 Knee hyperextension with a varus moment and
noncontact knee hyperextension in combination with external rotation also have been
described.7 Any type of knee dislocation can cause PLC injury, and an increase in low-
energy knee dislocations has been reported.19 Underlying varus alignment may
predispose patients to chronic PLC injuries.10

Concurrent ACL/PCL injuries
Peroneal nerve injury
Meniscal tear
Vascular injury in patients with a knee dislocation

bicruciate injuries is common. Studies report 15% to 29% of patients with a PLC injury
have peroneal nerve symptoms.20,21
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Lateral ligament injuries result from a direct medial or anteromedial blow or force to the
weight-bearing knee, resulting in excessive varus stress, external tibial rotation, and/or
hyperextension.7,10
A posterolaterally directed force to the medial tibia with the knee in extension is the most
common mechanism of injury.10
Combined injury to the cruciate ligaments is more common than isolated injury to the lateral
and posterolateral structures.2
Instability in active patients usually is noted with the knee near full extension. Patients may
have difficulty ascending/descending stairs and during cutting and/or pivoting.
Patients usually report lateral joint line pain after an acute injury.

Patient History
Patients will present in the acute setting with ecchymosis and pain after a sports injury,
motor vehicle collision, or fall. Patients who present chronically often report lateral- and
medial-based knee pain, ambulate with a varus thrust, and report a remote history of
prior knee trauma.

Physical Examination
Several special tests specific to the PLC are conducted in addition to basic palpation,
range of motion, and strength. An examination of the contralateral extremity is
important to establish a patient’s baseline. Varus stress testing at 30° primarily assesses
the LCL, whereas full extension testing assesses the LCL and associated cruciate
ligament injury. The Dial test is performed with the patient in the prone or supine
position with the knees flexed first at 30° and then at 90°, with an external rotation force
applied bilaterally at both angles. A difference of more than 10° at 30° of flexion
traditionally is consistent with an isolated PLC injury, whereas more than 10° of
asymmetry in external rotation at 90° is consistent with PLC and PCL injury.9 Wroble et
al23 reported a positive dial test in patients with a PLC injury and a concurrent ACL injury
if testing at 90° of flexion. The dial test may result in a false-positive result in patients
with a MCL injury.24

The external rotation and recurvatum test is performed with the patient in the supine
position. The examiner lifts the lower extremities by the forefoot. Combined knee
recurvatum and increased external rotation relative to the contralateral knee is
indicative of a PLC injury and may indicate a combined ACL/PLC injury.25,26 The
posterolateral drawer test is specific for rotatory injury to the PLC. The knee is held in
90° of flexion with the foot flat and externally rotated 15° on the examination table. The
knee is translated and rotated posterolaterally, causing the tibia to subluxate posteriorly
and laterally relative to the femur. A positive test has a soft endpoint with more than 3
mm of side-to-side difference compared with the uninjured knee.25 To perform the
reverse pivot-shift test, the knee is moved from flexion to extension with the foot held in
external rotation as a valgus force is applied. The result is positive if the tibia reduces
with a shift or jump from its posteriorly subluxated position at 20° to 30° of flexion. The
popliteal and iliotibial band are responsible for this reduction of the tibia. This test
should be performed on the contralateral knee because as many as 35% of normal
knees have a positive reverse pivot-shift test, which is observed in knees with some
aspect of recurvatum.27
Gait should be assessed as a varus or hyperextension thrust observed during the stance
phase of the gait cycle and may indicate a chronic PLC injury. Neurovascular injuries (ie,
common peroneal nerve injury associated with injuries to the LCL and PLC and popliteal
neurovascular injuries after a knee dislocation) are associated with specific patterns of
knee ligament injuries. A thorough neurovascular evaluation of the affected leg is
imperative because 15% of patients with an acute PLC injury have peroneal nerve
deficits. In addition, given the association with vascular injuries, the ABI should be
obtained in patients in whom a PLC or multiligamentous knee injury is suspected
regardless of the age of injury.

Radiography
Plain radiographs should be obtained for all patients in whom injury to the PLC is
suspected to rule out an associated osteochondral fracture, fibular head avulsion, Gerdy
tubercle avulsion, and/or fracture of the tibial plateau. Chronic posterolateral instability
may result in lateral tibiofemoral or patellofemoral degenerative changes. Weight-
bearing hip-to-ankle alignment radiographs are an important component of the
radiographic workup for chronic injuries because underlying varus malalignment may
increase the risk of failure after PLC reconstruction.10

Stress radiographs are effective in defining the nature of PLC injuries. LaPrade et al28
reported that normal physiologic gapping is 9.7 mm on a varus stress radiograph. If the
LCL is sectioned, an additional 2.7 mm of gapping occurs; if all three static stabilizers of
the lateral knee are sectioned, a total of 4 mm of additional gapping is observed. This
finding has questioned the traditional grading scheme because this study demonstrated
that only an additional 4 mm of lateral gapping is required for complete incompetence of
the PLC. Posterior stress radiographs are important to evaluate for PCL and PLC injuries.
Jackman et al29 demonstrated that an increase in posterior tibial subluxation of 12 mm
was consistent with combined PCL and PLC injury.
Computed Tomography
CT is useful in patients in whom fracture is suspected.
CT angiography is useful in patients in whom vascular injury is suspected.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is the preferred imaging modality to evaluate the status of the LCL, PLC, ACL/PCL, and
menisci.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Fine-cut (2 mm or less) slices with coronal oblique images are essential to provide an
entire view of the fibular head and the styloid.30 A coronal oblique MRI improves
visualization of the popliteal tendon. Bone contusion of the anteromedial femoral
condyle often is observed in patients with a PLC injury.1 MRI is a helpful imaging
modality in the acute setting; however, in the chronic setting, radiographs are most
helpful in the clinical decision-making process for management.

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Nonsurgical management of ligamentous injuries to the lateral side of the knee is limited to
partial (grade I and grade II) isolated injuries of the LCL.

Indications
Successful nonsurgical management of grade I PLC injuries and some grade II injuries
has been reported in the literature. Krukhaug et al31 reported successful nonsurgical
management of grade I injuries via early mobilization in a brace. Kannus32 published a
series on grade II and grade III PLC injuries and found that grade II injuries resulted in
good outcomes without surgical management despite some residual varus laxity,
whereas grade III injuries resulted in consistently poor outcomes.
Contraindications
Grade III injuries
Grade II injuries in combination with other ligamentous injury
Grade II avulsion injuries in high-demand patients

Contraindications
Nonsurgical management of grade III injuries generally is associated with poor clinical
outcomes.32 Rotatory knee laxity should compel strong consideration for surgical

Techniques/Procedures
Nonsurgical management consists of limited immobilization with protected–weight bearing for
the first 2 weeks. Progressive range of motion, quadriceps strengthening, and functional
rehabilitation are then initiated as tolerated.

Techniques/Procedures
Patients are protected from weight bearing and immobilized for 2 to 4 weeks in
extension, with quadriceps activation and straight-leg raises only. Beginning at weeks 2
to 4, protected range of motion in a hinged knee brace is initiated, and weight bearing is
advanced as tolerated. Physical therapy should avoid hamstring activation and focus on
closed kinetic chain quadriceps strengthening.10 Return to sports activity can be
expected at 6 to 8 weeks, depending on the sport and position played.
Surgical Management
Indications
Complete tears or avulsions of the LCL
Combined instability patterns involving the LCL/PLC and cruciate ligaments

Indications
The degree of rotatory instability is critical to determine because this component of
instability is more commonly missed. Some patient factors must be considered in those
with a grade II injury because high-demand athletes attempting to return to athletic
competition may not tolerate nonsurgical treatment. Assessment of anatomic alignment
is critical, especially in the chronic setting.33 Acute reconstruction should be performed

Techniques/Procedures
Patient Positioning
Supine, such that the surgical extremity can be comfortably flexed to 90°
Surgical Approach
Lateral, hockey-stick incision centered over the iliotibial band proximally to the midpoint
between the fibular head and the Gerdy tubercle

Surgical Approach
Before initiation of the open approach to the PLC, diagnostic arthroscopy is
recommended to assess intracapsular structures. In patients with posterior capsular
disruptions observed on MRI, caution should be exercised in undertaking prolonged
intra-articular procedures, which involve a risk for fluid extravasation into the leg. A
lateral, hockey-stick incision, typically measuring 12 to 18 cm in length, is used. The
common peroneal nerve is most reliably located proximally along the posterior aspect of
the biceps femoris, and complete neurolysis is performed. Commonly, the fascia of the
anterior compartment distally is opened to ensure the peroneal nerve is fully
decompressed along its course throughout the surgical exposure.
Surgical Procedures
Primary, acute repair of femoral- or tibial-sided avulsions
Reconstruction of midsubstance and/or chronic tears

In patients without considerable soft-tissue injury, swelling, and/or ecchymosis about the
knee, surgical management of the PLC within the first 3 weeks postinjury may be
advisable.10 In patients with an acute avulsion of the PLC structures, primary anatomic
repair may be considered. Reconstruction is indicated in patients in whom midsubstance
tears are present in acute or chronic situations. Several reconstruction techniques have
been described. The LaPrade PLC reconstruction technique is a two-graft construct
(Figure 6): the first graft runs from the LCL femoral origin through the fibular head in an
anterolateral to posteromedial fashion before it is docked with the second graft into a
posterior-to-anterior tunnel on the tibia. The purpose of the first graft is to re-create the
LCL and the popliteofibular ligament. The second graft starts at the popliteal origin on
the femur and travels posteriorly and inferiorly, at which it docks in the tibial tunnel with
the first graft.35

meniscal tears. Anteromedial rotatory instability generally is not well tolerated.65 If these
injuries go undiagnosed and patients are treated nonsurgically, the risk of persistent
instability is increased.

Stiffness
Standardized rehabilitation protocols focused on early range of motion and
strengthening have reduced the degree of stiffness; however, surgeons should ensure
patients are receiving the physical therapy they require. Close monitoring of patients
postoperatively is important to prevent arthrofibrosis. Manipulation under anesthesia
may be performed early in the postoperative course in patients who do not regaining
expected motion. Westermann et al66 performed a retrospective review of patients with
a grade III MCL injury in the setting of a surgically managed concomitant ACL rupture
and reported that revision surgery rates for arthrofibrosis increased from 9% to 19% in
patients with a surgically managed MCL injury. Limited data exist on the rate of
arthrofibrosis in patients who undergo isolated MCL reconstruction.
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Injury to the saphenous nerve may be temporary (neurapraxia) if it is stretched or permanent
(axonotmesis) if it is cut.

Nonsurgical management
Grade I injuries result in minimal swelling or effusion. A large effusion indicates a grade II
injury and/or concurrent ligamentous or cartilaginous injury. Grade III injuries may be
associated with disruption of the joint capsule, which allows joint fluid to track distally along
the anteromedial tibia.
MRI is indicated for a substantial effusion, an inconclusive physical examination of the
cruciate ligaments, or suspicion of a concurrent meniscal or cartilaginous injury.
The timing of return to sports activity is related directly to the degree of injury.
Grade I: 2 to 4 weeks
Grade II: 4 to 6 weeks
Grade III: 6 to 8 weeks
The timing of ACL reconstruction in patients with a concurrent MCL injury should be delayed
proportional to the degree of the MCL injury to allow for ligamentous healing (approximately
3 to 4 weeks for grade I, 4 to 6 weeks for grade II, and 6 to 8 weeks for grade III).
Surgical management
MRI may be useful in planning a limited surgical exposure based on the location of injury
(proximal or distal).
In patients undergoing primary repair or ligament reconstruction, a surgical tactic focused on
restoring native anatomy is critical. Failure to perform primary repair or reconstruction in an
anatomic fashion may jeopardize restoration of normal joint mobility.
